en: The *Sūtra on the Original Four Sons of Śreṇika*, spoken by the Buddha, translated by the lay devotee Zhi Qian of the Yuezhi country during the Wu dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Śāketa, traveling toward Kapilavastu.
In the Nyagrodha Grove of the Kauśāmbī kingdom, the Buddha was seated beneath a tree.
At that time, there was a Śākya named Maṇḍika who approached the Buddha, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet as a mark of reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I have often heard the words of the Buddha, and I have always kept them in my mind."
"I have heard the Buddha teach that there are three states of mind in human beings: the state of lust, the state of anger, and the state of delusion.
Since I first heard this, I have constantly applied my attention, thinking to myself:
'When there is no state of lust, the mind is naturally upright; when there is no state of anger, the mind is naturally upright; when there is no state of delusion, the mind is naturally upright.'"
I thought to myself:
"I constantly maintain these three things with an unshakable mind; for what reason and by what causal conditions do I still not understand? The Buddha said:
"If one has liberated oneself from lustful thoughts, angry thoughts, and deluded thoughts, for what reason would one still dwell together with wife and children?
It is because of the presence of greed. A worthy person reflects thus:"

"Although there is indeed a slight suffering for a short time, there will be great happiness later; whereas dwelling with one's wife and children brings only momentary pleasure for a brief while, there will be great suffering later.
"Is there anyone who is wise enough to know that worldly pleasures are few and sufferings are many?"
The Buddha said:
“The bhikṣus who have attained the path of arhatship know that there is little pleasure and much suffering in the world.
It is precisely because I contemplate how there is little pleasure and much suffering in the world that I sought the path of a Buddha.”
"When I was a bodhisattva, I constantly reflected that pleasure is little and suffering is much.
Mānava said, "Is it only the Buddha and the Arhats who have such a reflection?"
The Buddha told Maṇava:
“Listen to my words and take them to heart.
Among people in this world, what constitutes happiness?”
There are five kinds of pleasures that people crave and delight in.
The eye craves beautiful forms;
these become attached within the mind, and one thinks of them day and night with an attachment to beautiful forms.

When the ears hear pleasant sounds, the nose smells pleasant fragrances, the tongue delights in exquisite flavors, and the body obtains fine, soft textures, these immediately attach themselves to the mind, leading to craving for beautiful forms.
These five things are what the people of the world crave; all the pleasures and attachments of the world arise from these five matters.
Knowing this, how much sorrow could possibly arise?
People of the world may live by farming, or live by being craftsmen, or live by trading in markets, or live by serving as officials, or live by raising livestock, or live by being painters.

When such a person is cold, they endure the cold; when hot, they endure the heat; when suffering, they endure suffering; when hungry, they endure hunger; when thirsty, they endure thirst. Sitting together with a greedy mind, they collectively endure this cold, warmth, hunger, and thirst.
He lamented to himself:
"I have worked for many years, suffering as if I were dying, yet I have gained no wealth at all; I dwell amidst cold and hardship, and am even afflicted by illness and emaciation."
The Buddha told Maṇibhadra:
"This is the first suffering.
As for the second matter, it is the mind of lustful craving."

Among them, some become farmers, some become craftsmen, some become merchants, some become high officials, some become herdsmen, and some become painters; they engage in worldly livelihoods, enduring cold, heat, hunger, and thirst, driven by greed for wealth.

Having attained wealth and abundance, they further harbor anxiety and fear: fearing that government officials will seize their money and property; or fearing that a fire will break out and burn their money and property; or fearing that while traveling by boat, it will sink and they will lose their money and property; or fearing that bandits will plunder their money and property; or fearing that through trade or sale, they will lose their money and property; or fearing that impoverished relatives will administer poison to them; or fearing that their own children will disperse and squander their money and property. Such people constantly dwell with heavy sorrow, harboring anxiety day and night without a moment of relief.

Furthermore, suppose there is a person carrying wealth who encounters government officials, or fire and water; or whose goods are sold but not returned; or who buries them in the ground and forgets their location; or who is falsely accused and slandered; or whose own children spend his father’s wealth. That person thinks to himself:
"Since my youth I have managed my livelihood, enduring cold and heat, hunger and thirst, and suffering through toil to acquire this wealth, yet now it has been lost."

"From this anxiety, one may fall ill or die, all because of wealth and money; these are all brought about by the greedy mind and the five sensual pleasures. This constitutes the second suffering. Regarding the third matter:

people of the world, on account of money, quarrel—fathers with sons, elder brothers with younger brothers, husbands with wives, or acquaintances and friends with one another, or members of various families, both inside and out, quarreling with each other and speaking of their hidden faults behind their backs. All of these are brought about by the pursuit of pleasure through greed."

Because worldly people are bound by wealth and possessions, kings fight with kings, practitioners with practitioners, farmers with farmers, and artisans with artisans; all these arise from being bound by wealth. Thus they revile one another with their mouths, strike one another with staves, hack one another with blades, or even wound and kill one another—all of which is caused by greed. This constitutes the third suffering.
"Regarding the four matters: when people of the world enlist in the military, they receive official stipends with public knowledge that they must go to battle where life and death are uncertain;

it is all because of greed that they enlist. Having received the official stipends, they cannot stop and must fight. They may have their heads wounded or severed, their arms wounded or severed, or their feet wounded or severed; they exhaust one another in taking each other's lives—all of this is brought about by greed. These are the four sufferings."

"As for the five matters: there are those in the world whose minds are greedy who, traveling by night, tunnel through the walls of others' houses, or plunder people on the roads, or attack their cities and strongholds. When they are captured by the officials, some have their heads cut off, some have their hands cut off, some have their feet cut off, some are dismembered, some have their flesh sliced, some are burned with fire, some have their foreheads struck with heavy mallets, and some have their waists severed—all of these are brought about by a greedy mind; these constitute the five sufferings."

"People of the world sit upon wealth and property, deceiving one another through speech, deceiving one another through body, and deceiving one another through mind. At such times, they consider themselves capable of acting as they please, believing themselves to be without fault or transgression;
yet they do not realize that the calamity and poison lie ahead, and that they shall enter hell."
"Suppose there were such as a noble one, or a śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa, who reflected for themselves: 'In this world, are the five pleasures many, or are sorrow and suffering many?
The Buddha said to Maṇava:
"When I was a bodhisattva, I constantly reflected that there is little happiness and much suffering in the world; for this reason, I sought the path of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Anyone who would claim that there is happiness in the world does not understand the way of birth and death."
"If there is one in the world who is virtuous and good, whose mind is free from the will of greed, and who further desires to teach others not to be greedy, this person is the most highly virtuous.
The Buddha told Maṇava:
"I once went to the kingdom of Rājagṛha; there was a mountain named Saptaparṇa where the couple Ghoṭamukha and Bhāradvāja practiced giving."

I have seen various followers of the Nirgrantha sect—some who go about with disheveled hair, some who walk hunched over, some who sit upon the ground, and some who lie upon the ground; their bodies are unclothed, all wearing deerskins.
The Buddha saw them from afar and went forward to speak with the Nirgranthas:
"For what cause and condition do you go about with your hair disheveled?
For what cause and condition do you sit and lie upon the ground, without clothing or coverings, tormenting yourselves in this way?"
The Nigaṇṭhas replied to the Buddha:
"It is due to the evil deeds committed by us in previous lives that we suffer such hardship in this present life; it is simply because our past evil karma has not yet been exhausted."
The Buddha said:
"By what causes and conditions did you come to know that this matter was done in a previous life?
Did you hear it from someone?"
"Do you know of this yourself?
The Nirgranthas replied,
"We do not know it, nor have we heard of it, nor do we serve a teacher."
The Buddha said:
"If you undergo such hardship and suffering for this reason, will you thereby be liberated from birth and death?
If you neither hear the Dharma from others nor serve a teacher, what is the use of subjecting yourself to empty hardship?"
"It would be better for you to abandon what you are doing and come to serve the Buddha-way.
The Buddha said, "I merely cherish your person and am mindful of your descendants; in future generations, they shall all return to the Dharma and emulate the deeds of those like you."
All the Nirgranthas became enraged at what the Buddha had said, exclaiming:
"King Bimbisāra has taken this śramaṇa Gautama into his kingdom!
The Buddha addressed the Nirgranthas:
"Do not be angry! King Pīṇḍola has accepted my sūtra; perhaps he does not dare to speak falsely.
The Buddha then addressed the Nirgranthas:
"Can you all truly sit upright for seven days and seven nights, without food or drink and without speech, and find such a thing pleasurable?
Or is it the palaces, courtyards, and music of the king that you consider pleasure?"
The Nirgrantha said:
"Śramaṇa Gautama! It is for the sake of pleasure."
The Buddha asked:
"What do you consider to be happiness?
Why is it that King Bimbisāra does not find happiness in his kingdom?"
The Nirgranthas said, "We have little concern; for this reason, the śramaṇa Gautama has surpassed King Bimbisāra.
The Buddha addressed the Nirgranthas:
"King Bimbisāra!

You possess thoughts of lust, thoughts of anger, and thoughts of delusion; furthermore, you desire to subdue your ministers and also desire to subdue the subjects outside. Day and night you calculate and deliberate: 'Whom shall I punish? Whom shall I imprison?'"
The Buddha said:
"Those who harbor lust also wish to kill themselves and wish to kill others;
those who harbor anger also wish to kill themselves and wish to kill others."
"The deluded person desires both to kill themselves and to kill others.

All the Nirgranthas then went before the Buddha and said to him, "We are likewise free from lustful tendencies, free from angry tendencies, and free from deluded tendencies; we would surely be able to become śramaṇas."
The Buddha said,
"You should return and inform your parents.
The Nirgranthas said:
"We have left our homes to study the Way; we have already taken our leave of our parents.
The Buddha said, "For now, you all should receive the five precepts and return home."
All the Nirgranthas received the five precepts: first, not to kill; second, not to steal; third, not to violate the wives of others; fourth, not to deceive; and fifth, not to drink alcohol.
"The various Nirgranthas have received the five precepts; they wear their robes, keep their hair tied up, and practice upright conduct, each returning to their own homes.
The Buddha told Maṇava:

"If you hear of lustful thoughts, angry thoughts, or deluded thoughts within the sutras, or if you say, 'I uphold the Buddha's teachings,' then reflect deeply upon these five matters: are they not equal to those of the world?"
Mānava said, "I shall return to contemplate, recite, and chant this sūtra, and I will go to the Buddha's dwelling today.
Having paid homage to the Buddha, Mānava departed.
The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Original Four Sons of Śreṇika Mānava.
